title: Lift a dish drainer's folded plate rack until it locks, then stand two plates in it
instruction: Put the two washed plates in the draining board's plate rack: lift the rack until it locks upright, then stand each plate on edge in a different slot, and let go.
context: Anyone who washes up by hand ends by standing the clean plates on edge in a drainer's plate rack so they drain. A fold-flat draining board is stored with its plate rack folded down, so the first step is to lift the rack until it locks upright: an unlocked rack folds back under a plate and the plate falls flat. Here the washed plates were propped on the sink's back upstand because the rack was still folded. A plate can only be pinched by its top rim, so it hangs below the hand with its 22 mm deep dished body behind the pinch: it is carried beside the rack, slid in along its own plane between two prongs with 5 mm to spare each side, set on the deck, tipped onto a prong and let go. Two plates in one slot grind and chip; a plate dropped or laid flat does not drain.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; the table top (a kitchen counter) is the reference height. x points forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the left of the midpoint between them, z up; arm bases at y +30.5 cm and -30.5 cm. (1) A Joseph Joseph Flip-Up draining board (grey, 319 x 400 mm), fixed: x 26 to 345 mm, y -200 to +200 mm, its deck 12 mm over the counter. Its white plate rack is a hinge bar along x at y +80 mm, 16 mm up, carrying seven prongs 8 mm square and 95 mm long at x 90, 130, 170, 210, 250, 290 and 330 mm. At the start the rack lies folded flat on the deck, prongs pointing -y (tips at y -19 mm). Lifted, it turns about the bar to upright (prong tops 115 mm over the counter; a stop 2 degrees past upright). Within 5 degrees of upright its lock holds it at 90 degrees; elsewhere it sinks back flat under its own weight. Upright, the prongs make six slots 32 mm wide, centred x 110, 150, 190, 230, 270 and 310 mm. (2) The sink unit's steel back upstand, fixed: 10 mm thick, 75 mm tall, y -200 to +600 mm, its front face at x 351 mm. A tiled splashback, fixed: 300 mm tall, front face at x 450 mm. The sink's steel rim on the counter at x 100 to 395 mm, y -620 to -240 mm, with a mixer tap 250 mm tall at x 420, y -430 mm. (3) Two Corelle Winter Frost White 6.75 in bread and butter plates, 171 mm across, 22 mm deep, 0.130 kg each, dished: a flat well 110 mm across, a sloping wall and a flat rim 14 mm wide, 4 mm walls. Each leans back on the upstand's top front edge, 12 degrees from vertical, face toward the robot (-x), its lowest point on the counter at x 317 mm: plate 1 centred y +265 mm, plate 2 centred y +450 mm (outlines 14 mm apart). A plate is picked up by its top rim (gripper opening 94 mm) and hangs below the hand. Standing in a slot on the deck it has 5 mm to each prong and comes to rest leaning on a prong at up to 21 degrees (about 15 where the demo sets it). Nothing else is on the counter.
scoring: End state, read at the last step from the poses of the plates, the rack's angle and both grippers. The rack is up when it is 85 degrees or more from flat. A plate is placed when the rack is up and: its lowest point is within 5 mm of the deck; every point of the plate within 10 mm of its lowest point lies between the inner faces of one slot's two prongs, 0.5 mm allowed; its plane is within 25 degrees of vertical; and its centre line is 30 to 70 mm beyond the prong row (y 110 to 150 mm), so the prongs cross it well inside its rim. A plate is upright when its plane is within 40 degrees of vertical. Hands off: on every step of the last 1 s both grippers' finger zones are 30 mm or more from both plates and the rack, and no point of either plate or of the rack moves 2 mm or more (a plate's top rim and the prong tips move most when a plate tips or the rack sags). Score 0 if at any step a plate moves down at 0.9 m/s or faster (41 mm of free fall reaches that speed; read 20 times a second, every fall of 100 mm or more is caught) or its lowest point drops 20 mm below the counter; 0 unless hands off; 0 unless the rack is up. Otherwise: 1.0 both plates placed, in different slots; 0.5 one slot holds a placed plate (or both are placed in the same slot) and every plate is upright; 0.25 no plate placed and every plate upright (the rack raised and locked, nothing in it), or one plate placed and the other lying down; 0 otherwise. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0. The path, the order of the plates and which arm does what are not scored. Success: 1.0 held for 1 s. In a real trial: rack up, a phone level on a prong (85 degrees) and the lock engaged; lowest point, a 5 mm feeler gauge under the plate; between prongs, by eye from above against the two prongs; tilt, a phone level on the plate's face (25 and 40 degrees); centre line, a ruler from the prong row (30 to 70 mm); hands off, a 30 mm spacer block against each hand; still, a sticker dot on each plate's top rim and on both end prongs' tips, filmed at 30 fps from the front and from the side beside a mm rule, no dot moving 2 mm over the last 1 s; fall, 30 fps video against a rule (a plate moving down 30 mm or more between two frames, 0.9 m/s); counter, by eye.
fidelity: Rigid bodies. The plates are the real dished shape as boxes (well, sloping wall, flat rim; profile est). The board is fixed (real: non-slip feet). The rack's lock is a rule on its hinge: within 5 degrees of upright it holds at 90, else it sinks flat. Prong size, pitch and the deck height are est (the maker lists no slot sizes); friction est; plates dry. The sink bowl is a dark patch in its rim. Side plates, not dinner plates: a hanging dinner plate is beyond the arms' height.
reset_notes: Fold the rack flat on the deck, prongs toward the sink (-y). Lean each plate back on the upstand's top front edge, 12 degrees from vertical, face toward the robot, its lowest point at x 317 mm: plate 1 centred y +265 mm, plate 2 centred y +450 mm. The board, upstand, splashback, sink rim and tap stay fixed. Wipe the plates dry; replace a chipped plate, as a chip changes the rim the pads grip.
